Second-line Parkinson's disease patients (previously on ropinirole) tolerated the switch to rotigotine transdermal patch with 80% completion rate and minimal cardiovascular changes. Secondary motor (UPDRS -1.9) and QoL (PDQ-8 -3.9) endpoints showed directional improvement but no p-values were reported and there is no comparator arm, limiting confidence. The signal is directionally positive but weak.

The partial improvements in UPDRS Part III (-1.9) and PDQ-8 (-3.9) after switching to rotigotine suggest maintained dopaminergic neurotransmission restoration, consistent with receptor agonism driving the intended biology. However, single-arm design and absence of p-values limit confidence in this causal attribution.

Directional improvements in motor function (UPDRS Part III) and quality of life (PDQ-8) after switching to rotigotine are consistent with dopaminergic neurotransmission restoration driving Parkinson's disease symptom control. The effect sizes are small and no statistical testing was reported, and the single-arm design precludes strong causal inference.
